cards.answer_text:
For most remote Docker Engine access, use SSH rather than exposing an unauthenticated TCP API. The remote account must be allowed to access the Docker socket. Create and select a context, then test it:

```console
docker context create --docker host=ssh://docker-user@host1.example.com --description="Remote engine" my-remote-engine
docker context use my-remote-engine
docker info
```

`docker info` should show information from the remote engine. Switch back with `docker context use default`. For a temporary connection without a context, use `export DOCKER_HOST=ssh://docker-user@host1.example.com` and then run a Docker CLI command such as `docker info`.

If you specifically need TCP/HTTPS, configure the daemon for TLS verification with a trusted CA, server certificate/key, and a TCP listener (the docs use port 2376); connect with client certificates and verify the server certificate. Protect those keys carefully. Remote access without TLS is not recommended: the daemon documentation warns that unsecured access can allow remote users to gain host root access. Don't configure the systemd unit and `daemon.json` to set the same listener, as that conflict prevents Docker from starting.

cards.answer_text:
Install/use the Go Engine SDK (`github.com/moby/moby/client`; the docs show `go get github.com/moby/moby/client`) and run the program with Docker available. The quickstart flow pulls Alpine, creates a container whose command is `echo hello world`, starts it, waits for completion, then reads stdout logs. Here is that flow with basic error checks and API negotiation enabled:

```go
package main

import (
	"context"
	"io"
	"os"

	"github.com/moby/moby/api/pkg/stdcopy"
	"github.com/moby/moby/api/types/container"
	"github.com/moby/moby/client"
)

func must(err error) {
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
}

func main() {
	ctx := context.Background()
	cli, err := client.New(client.FromEnv, client.WithAPIVersionNegotiation())
	must(err)
	defer cli.Close()

	pull, err := cli.ImagePull(ctx, "docker.io/library/alpine", client.ImagePullOptions{})
	must(err)
	_, err = io.Copy(os.Stdout, pull)
	must(err)
	must(pull.Close())

	created, err := cli.ContainerCreate(ctx, client.ContainerCreateOptions{
		Image: "alpine",
		Config: &container.Config{
			Cmd: []string{"echo", "hello world"},
		},
	})
	must(err)
	_, err = cli.ContainerStart(ctx, created.ID, client.ContainerStartOptions{})
	must(err)

	wait := cli.ContainerWait(ctx, created.ID, client.ContainerWaitOptions{})
	select {
	case err := <-wait.Error:
		must(err)
	case <-wait.Result:
	}

	logs, err := cli.ContainerLogs(ctx, created.ID, client.ContainerLogsOptions{ShowStdout: true})
	must(err)
	defer logs.Close()
	_, err = stdcopy.StdCopy(os.Stdout, os.Stderr, logs)
	must(err)
}
```

`client.FromEnv` reads the Docker connection configuration; for Docker Desktop for Linux, set `DOCKER_HOST=unix://$HOME/.docker/desktop/docker.sock` in the process environment. Desktop for Linux uses this per-user socket rather than the system-wide `/var/run/docker.sock`. The SDK install page also says to use a recent, currently supported Go version. [SDK quickstart, lines 22–40, 46–60, 62–74](content_reference_api_engine_sdk_quickstart__e94c7e9c); [SDK install, lines 10–20, 35–44](content_reference_api_engine_sdk_install__7cca9109)

For differing client and daemon versions, check `docker version` to see each side's API support. The guidance is to use the latest SDK and enable API negotiation: it selects the highest API version supported by both client and daemon. Downgrading disables later API features, and compatibility is best-effort, so verify your smoke test on the actual daemon(s). Avoid setting `DOCKER_API_VERSION` unless you need to force a particular version: it disables negotiation. [Version guidance and check, lines 29–32, 61–66](content_reference_api_engine_versioning__f9c03b91); [negotiation and forced-version behavior, lines 75–97, 106–118](content_reference_api_engine_versioning__f9c03b91)

The Go sample follows the documented quickstart, which waits for the container and then fetches logs. It does not inspect the wait result's exit status; if the test must assert a successful exit (not just completion and output), additionally check the returned wait status code before treating the smoke test as passed. The cited quickstart demonstrates receiving the result but does not document that assertion. [Quickstart, lines 60–74](content_reference_api_engine_sdk_quickstart__e94c7e9c)

cards.answer_text:
Yes. Docker Desktop sign-in enforcement can require members to authenticate as members of your Docker organization before using Desktop. By default, organization members can use Desktop without signing in; non-member sign-ins are automatically rejected, and signing out makes Desktop unusable until they sign back in. This enforcement is separate from SSO: use SSO enforcement too if you want to require identity-provider authentication. (It does not restrict Docker CLI access unless your organization enforces SSO.)

For a cross-platform deployment, use `registry.json`: create the file at the platform’s documented location (Windows: `/ProgramData/DockerDesktop/registry.json`; Mac: `/Library/Application Support/com.docker.docker/registry.json`; Linux: `/usr/share/docker-desktop/registry/registry.json`), add `{"allowedOrgs":["your-org"]}`, set permissions to prevent user editing, then restart Docker Desktop. Confirm the `Sign in required!` prompt appears. Windows-only registry-key and Mac-only configuration-profile or `.plist` methods are also documented; configuration profiles are recommended for Mac.

Benefits include ensuring users receive subscription benefits, applying organization security features, and gaining insight into user activity. Without member sign-in, users may miss subscription benefits and circumvent security features. For SSO enforcement, the documented additional benefits are centralized authentication and identity-provider policies.

No—not completely by SSO alone. Docker’s default SSO provisioning is JIT; SCIM is the mechanism for ongoing user provisioning/deprovisioning, profile updates, and group mapping. With SCIM enabled, Docker syncs users provisioned through the IdP, but it does not remove users who were manually added before SCIM was set up (those must be removed manually). [SCIM overview, lines 39–57](content_manuals_enterprise_security_provisioning_scim_index__b0957a6a)

For ongoing sync, configure SCIM in Docker and your IdP, and ensure the relevant users/groups are assigned. Also check JIT attribute mappings: JIT values take precedence over SCIM values, so keep them aligned or disable JIT to rely solely on SCIM. [SCIM setup, lines 47–64](content_manuals_enterprise_security_provisioning_scim_provision_scim__55cf107e)

Group/team changes sync only when group mapping is configured correctly; the IdP must send group information, and the setup should be tested. [Group mapping, lines 40–58](content_manuals_enterprise_security_provisioning_scim_group_mapping__a9ca0024) You can test provisioning on demand in the IdP and confirm the user appears under Docker Admin Console → Members; check the IdP provisioning logs if it does not. [SCIM test steps, lines 341–365](content_manuals_enterprise_security_provisioning_scim_provision_scim__55cf107e)

cards.answer_text:
Use LocalStack in a Testcontainers-managed test container so the Spring AWS clients target the emulator, not AWS. Add the Spring Cloud AWS S3 and SQS starters, the Testcontainers LocalStack module, and Awaitility for asynchronous SQS assertions; the guide’s sample uses Java 17, Testcontainers 2.0.4, and Spring Cloud AWS 3.0.3 (treat those as sample versions, and align them with your project’s compatibility requirements). [Project setup](content_guides_testcontainers_java_aws_localstack_create_project__e8f06dfd:28-33) [Sample versions](content_guides_testcontainers_java_aws_localstack_create_project__e8f06dfd:35-42)

In the test harness, declare a static `LocalStackContainer` with `@Container` and `@Testcontainers`, then use `@DynamicPropertySource` to supply Spring’s S3 and SQS endpoints from `localStack.getEndpointOverride(S3/SQS)`, along with the container’s region and credentials. This runtime wiring is important for parallel CI: do not rely on the guide’s illustrative fixed `localhost:4566` endpoint when the container is mapped to a random port. The guide explicitly recommends ephemeral containers on random available ports to avoid conflicts between parallel builds. [Container and dynamic endpoint wiring](content_guides_testcontainers_java_aws_localstack_write_tests__a973eb0f:57-93) [Illustrative properties and random-port guidance](content_guides_testcontainers_java_aws_localstack_write_tests__a973eb0f:16-29)

Give each test run unique bucket and queue names (the sample uses UUIDs), create those resources in LocalStack, then publish a message and poll until the expected S3 object content is present. That checks the SQS-to-application-to-S3 integration rather than merely checking that Spring starts. [Unique names and resource setup](content_guides_testcontainers_java_aws_localstack_write_tests__a973eb0f:61-105) [Publish and assert with Awaitility](content_guides_testcontainers_java_aws_localstack_write_tests__a973eb0f:116-131)

Run `./mvnw test` or `./gradlew test`. Verify in the test output that LocalStack starts and the test passes; the guide says the container stops and is removed automatically afterward. It also describes these tests as using ephemeral containers on random ports with no external setup. [Run and cleanup check](content_guides_testcontainers_java_aws_localstack_run_tests__51513771:10-23) [Ephemeral/random-port summary](content_guides_testcontainers_java_aws_localstack_run_tests__51513771:27-30)

If local container workloads strain developer machines, evaluate Testcontainers Cloud as an option for offloading container management. The documentation says it frees local resources and offers isolated, consistent environments and scalability; its local setup walkthrough describes using Testcontainers Desktop and the CLI, and monitoring cloud containers. Try the same integration suite locally and with Cloud, comparing test duration, local resource use, and whether cleanup/monitoring meet your needs. The cited material describes benefits and setup at a high level; it does not establish pricing or a guarantee for your workload. [Cloud benefits](content_guides_testcontainers_cloud_why__f60529db:11-20) [Local setup and monitoring overview](content_guides_testcontainers_cloud_demo_local__a44d93c1:15-25)
